content: Vaccination policy refers to the strategies and practices implemented by governments regarding the administration of vaccines. In some countries, vaccination is voluntary, while in others, it is mandatory. Certain governments subsidize the cost of vaccines, either partially or fully, for those included in their national immunization schedules. Goals of Vaccination Policies Immunity and Herd Immunity The primary objective of vaccination policies is to establish immunity against specific diseases. Beyond protecting individuals from illness, some vaccination programs aim to achieve herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when a significant portion of the population becomes immune to a pathogen, thereby reducing its ability to spread within the community. Eradication of Disease For certain diseases, vaccination policies aim to completely eradicate the disease from the planet. A notable success story is the global eradication of smallpox, achieved through coordinated efforts led by the World Health Organization (WHO). The last naturally occurring case of smallpox was reported in Somalia in 1977. Similarly, Finland has successfully eliminated endemic measles, mumps, and rubella. While polio was targeted for eradication by the year 2000, this goal was not fully achieved. Measles is considered a potential next target for eradication, as its incidence has significantly declined since the introduction of the measles vaccine in 1963. Compulsory Vaccination as a Policy To minimize the risk of disease outbreaks, various governments and institutions have, at times, implemented mandatory vaccination policies. For instance, a law enacted in England and Wales in 1853 required universal smallpox vaccination, with fines imposed on those who failed to comply. In the United States, the Supreme Court ruled in the 1905 case Jacobson v. Commonwealth of Massachusetts that states could mandate vaccinations for the collective welfare. Today, many vaccination policies require children to receive standard immunizations before entering school. A few other countries also enforce mandatory vaccination for certain diseases. Mandatory vaccination has been credited with significantly reducing the prevalence of infectious diseases. However, such policies have historically faced resistance from groups collectively referred to as anti-vaccinationists. These groups have raised objections on ethical, political, medical safety, religious, and other grounds. Common criticisms include concerns about excessive government intervention in personal matters and doubts about the safety of certain vaccines. Modern vaccination policies often include exemptions for individuals with compromised immune systems, allergies to vaccine components, or deeply held personal objections. For example, in 1904, a government program in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, mandating smallpox vaccination led to the Vaccine Revolt, a series of riots that caused significant property damage and loss of life. The implementation of compulsory vaccination policies involves complex ethical considerations, as health authorities must balance societal health benefits with individual liberties and freedom of expression. Vaccination is unique in that it requires individuals to accept the injection of a medicinal agent into their bodies, which has historically provoked spirited opposition. This opposition began with the earliest vaccinations and continues to this day. Vaccination and School Attendance In the United States, all states have laws requiring children to be vaccinated according to CDC-recommended schedules as a prerequisite for school attendance. However, exemptions for religious, philosophical, or medical reasons are permitted in all states. Schools often require vaccinations for highly contagious diseases, such as Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) and chickenpox, to prevent significant disruptions during outbreaks. However, they are less likely to mandate vaccines for diseases like Hepatitis B, which is transmitted through blood and not casual classroom contact. The American Academy of Pediatrics has, in rare cases, considered parental refusal to vaccinate as a form of child neglect or abuse. Organizations opposed to mandatory vaccination often publicize the procedures for obtaining exemptions. The debate over mandatory vaccination policies continues to raise challenging questions about how public health authorities should address the anti-vaccination movement. A passive approach may risk public health, while an overly aggressive stance could infringe on individual freedoms and values.
